content: OSHA excavation rules require each employee in an excavation to be protected from cave-ins by an adequate protective system, except when excavation is entirely in stable rock or is less than five feet deep and a competent person finds no indication of a potential cave-in.
A stairway, ladder, ramp, or other safe means of egress must be located in trench excavations that are four feet or more in depth so employees need no more than twenty-five feet of lateral travel.

Protective systems for excavations deeper than twenty feet must be designed by a registered professional engineer or based on tabulated data prepared or approved by a registered professional engineer.

Base flood elevation is the elevation of surface water resulting from a flood with a one percent chance of equaling or exceeding that level in any given year. Floodplain design review compares proposed elevations with the mapped BFE.

FEMA technical bulletins provide guidance for compliant flood-resistant buildings, including elevation, flood damage-resistant materials, utilities, enclosures below elevated buildings, and wet or dry floodproofing.

Construction activities that disturb land and discharge stormwater may require Clean Water Act NPDES permit coverage. Operators must implement erosion and sediment controls and meet applicable stabilization requirements.

Construction stormwater best management practices include minimizing disturbed areas, preserving vegetation, controlling erosion and sediment, managing construction entrances, and stabilizing exposed soil.

The 2010 ADA Standards set technical requirements for accessible routes and ramps. Ramp runs generally have a maximum running slope of one to twelve and require compliant landings, clear width, edge protection, and handrails where applicable.

Curb ramps provide an accessible route between sidewalks and streets. Guidance addresses running slope, cross slope, detectable warnings, landings, and placement so a person using a wheelchair can travel safely.
